representative_reviews.title: To the Moon
representative_reviews.text: Let me start by stating that I love pixel art, rich soundtracks, and narrative-driven titles. To the Moon checks all three boxes. I first played this game in 2018. While its beautiful soundtrack stayed with me over the years, most of the plot had faded from memory. During a recent multi-hour train ride, I was scrolling through my Steam Deck library and rediscovered this gem. I decided to give it another shot, playing through both the main game and the two free "Sigmund Minisodes" DLCs. There is so much to love here. It’s a deeply emotional story about life, love, family, and loss, following a dying man and his late wife, alongside two doctors who rarely agree on anything but always have each other's backs when it counts. The soundtrack, in particular, is stunning and carries the weight of the narrative effortlessly. Just don't expect traditional gameplay. The experience consists almost entirely of searching for objects, clicking through environments, and solving the occasional light puzzle. It leans far closer to an interactive visual novel or walking simulator than a standard video game. Because it's relatively short, it never overstays its welcome. For me, replaying it was an absolute pleasure. The optional minisodes also add a fantastic touch, fleshing out Sigmund Corp., exploring its employees, and leaving you with a few intriguing mysteries to chew on. If you enjoy story-driven experiences with great art and music, and don't mind minimal gameplay, you owe it to yourself to give To the Moon a try.

representative_reviews.title: Finding Paradise
representative_reviews.text: [h2]A solid addition to the world of "To the moon"[/h2] I think if I had to pick, I'd probably say I preferred to the moon, but that could just as well be because I played it first, it's not uncommon to be biased towards your introductory game or episode of a series. I thought this was pretty sweet, it's still a narrative game with some puzzle elements, but the writing is great, if the writing wasn't as top tier as it is I definitely wouldn't have enjoyed this or to the moon one bit, and for a dyslexic person who struggles to maintain focus when reading, that says a lot to it's quality. The sprites are mostly just the same as to the moon, but still just as amazing, I did notice some weird mixels during Neil's transformation sequence, and some tiny spots where pixels didn't line up fully or were a bit jittery, nothing that'd ruin your experience but they did stick out to me during my playthrough. The music is phenomenal as you'd expect, maybe a bit samey at times, but better that than incohesive, a little more variety in some spots wouldn't hurt, and might heighten the impact of the emotional tracks when they come in, but again, nothing that'll detract from your experience. I played "A bird story" prior to this, and honestly I didn't quite get the connection, I mean, yeah, same character, it's a standalone look into a point of his life that's been abstracted, but for a chunk of the game I was just like "so she's the bird maybe?" But no, the bird is kind of just insignificant outside of "A bird story", which was kind of sad to me, but it is what it is, it's not like it ruined the experience for me. I think Asher could've done with a bit more character development maybe, more screentime, more moments with his family, but the story does go on a bit as is, so I'm not mad they didn't try to shove more in there; I [i]am[/i] mad about the walk speed though, it's just too slow, for "To the moon" I think it worked better because the environments were a bit smaller, sometimes you'd be on a long walk from one area to another, but having most segments be smaller walkable areas made the walk speed feel reasonable for the majority of it, here it felt like it was padding the length of the game a bit, a sprint button at least would've been appreciated, I'm not saying we need to be running the whole game, just a slight increase, because as is, I felt like the walkspeed alone added at least half an hour to my playtime, maybe even a whole hour. But overall, great game, I thought it was really sweet, teared up a little at the end, I had minimal gripes with the story, the art, the music, the gameplay, I'm not gonna pretend there wasn't any friction with any of it, but it's so minimal compared to the master craftsmanship behind the entire rest of the game that they're just insignificant. If you're not a narrative game type, or you prefer games with intricate gameplay mechanics, multiple routes or endings, maybe this won't be for you, but if you like a good story with some interactive elements, I think this is worth your time.

representative_reviews.title: Meg's Monster
representative_reviews.text: Overall I enjoyed the experience I had playing this game, though it was different than I expected it to be. I think anyone going into this should expect it be more like a visual novel than anything else. I feel like it's got something it's trying to be but doesn't really hit the mark. The art style and music aren't quite cozy and the dialogue goes from nearing cringe territory to quite hard hitting. The end gets very long as it repeats the scenes over and over again with slight variations and I didn't totally feel like it had been earned yet. I've seen other reviews complaining that the story is very linear, but I don't see that as a negative. Not every story needs explorations and million different endings and a billion things to do. If you want to play those games, then avoid this one and go play those. The combat only gets interesting in the end-game. It feels like it was added on and not intended for this game. I did find the mechanics a bit interesting but for the most part it's pretty simple to sort out a strategy that works most of the time. When they started throwing new things at me in the end-game it only took two or three tried to get the right combo/luck.

representative_reviews.title: In Stars And Time
representative_reviews.text: Playing this game was an experience I will never forget! :D The art and music draws you in, but the comradery between Isabeau, Odile, Mirabelle, Bonnie, and Siffrin as well as the twists and turns along the way keep you locked in. I had so much fun just reading the dialogue between characters. So much humor and charm behind nearly every interaction, even with the people in the town. Their friendship is an anchor in a world of chaos, and it's so wholesome despite the pressure they faced. I also liked how the battle system was based on rock. paper, scissors, even if it did make combat less complex as a turn-based game. My only gripe with the battle system was how tedious it became to battle over the course of the game. I eventually found an item that allowed me to circumvent some of the tediousness which was nice. My main complaint with the game is that there are certain parts that feel unnecessarily frustrating and difficult to complete. I would say Act 4 gave me the most trouble and I actually had to go through a walkthrough twice in order to finally pass it. The story, characters, art, and music make it worth it but it does feel a little too much at certain points even if I understand it relates to a core part of the story. I highly recommend this game! This is one of those games that can change your life by playing. I will never forget my buddies Siffrin, Odile, Isabeau, Mirabelle, and Bonnie ; u; <3

representative_reviews.title: In Stars And Time
representative_reviews.text: If there one characteristic I'm certain on, In Stars And Time's writing takes out many dialogue flourishes and facial expressions to make the characters WORK, especially across many, many, many, loops. Those interactions changing across the loops is how I see this story suits itself to a game. On the flipside, I not so sure I felt like gameplay should really take this long, owning to how combat is "required" with a certain fast traveling resource that feels somehow separate from the story, and yet is part of the story. I suppose that resource is just-- not gelling with the story in a game technical sense. I suppose, the story doesn't have much interactions with that resource outside of the resource being used to force the player to battle enemies? Except, enemies aren't *the* problem, rather it is the environment that acts as the challenge posed by the story. Enemies are just there, with very little interactions compared to the environment. With that said, I enjoyed In Stars And Times for bringing out these lovable dorks of main party, and an excellent showcase of dialogue tricks... Oh, I suppose I should say the game does a lot with very little in regards to maps & music. Classic pitch shifting, hahaha!

representative_reviews.title: Small Saga
representative_reviews.text: Yeah, it was okay. More theatrical than tactical, this game offers a casual RPG experience that is hard to lose at even if you find only the bare minimum in equippables yet contains enough content and sidequests to hold a seat at the table of the Game for RPG Players Union. Level ups come to the player at set points instead of through number gains (some of these set points are optional), battles will go by swiftly if you pay enough attention to the arrangement of skill points on your character grids (and they can be arranged freely), and the story plays out in a fashion meant for the coolness factor rather than in meaningful prose. It has nowhere else to go when it's about rodents looking to kill humans and only able to deal bare minimum damage even with a Swiss Army Knife, lol. Of course it contains a bunch of other inter-rodent strife and matching politics, some of them matching real life politics which will probably annoy you if you're not left-leaning, but nothing too serious. Come to this game if you'd like ten hours of fun, good music, and a decent narrative themed "no gods, no masters" to pass the time.

representative_reviews.title: Small Saga
representative_reviews.text: Very solid and fun RPG. Characters are lovable with cute designs and great writing with fun moments for all of the main party members and their various acquaintances. The game also does not hide its inspirations at all which can be pretty funny (such as the buff that the main character can apply to themselves after the prologue lol) It is a bit on the shorter side for an RPG, but it also doesn't waste your time with any grinding or tedious sidequests. Every fight you get into is relevant to the main story at hand, and you usually only have a handful of fights before you get to the next big Boss Fight. And the Bosses are universally really fun, usually sporting their own unique gimmicks to set each of those fights apart from each other. The side quests that do exist are few, but again, they don't waste your time and are very fun individual quests. The levelup system is also pretty simple too, but it gives you a good few ways to lean each of the characters in different directions. So I do feel like there's a good bit of agency. And I also love how the item system works, where once you get a consumable that can heal you or cure a status effect or something, you can just equip it to a party member, and then that person can always use that item once per fight, so you don't have to worry about running out of them or anything like that. My one complaint about the game is that I felt like by the end I got a bit too powerful for the game to handle. If you do all of the sidequests to unlock everyone's ultimate abilities, you can kinda become absurdly unstoppable and as a result the final boss was a little underwhelming since I was able to just blow right through it while barely taking any damage to my party. Other than that, like I said the game is fairly short, and I certainly wouldn't have complained if there were maybe 1 or 2 more seasons worth of content with a couple more story arcs to go through, but when my biggest complaint with a game is that I want more of it, that's usually a good sign. Overall very much worth the price of admission, and in many ways I think is also a good intro RPG to the genre if you're not as familiar with its conventions. But even as a long time fan of RPGs I still loved what it had to offer.

representative_reviews.title: Ikenfell
representative_reviews.text: I cannot recommend this game enough. The storytelling is compelling, the music is enthralling, the art is stunning, and the character development is so, so realistic. Conversely to many, I enjoyed the battle mechanics; I loved mixing & matching characters, and optimizing field movement. Moreover, I felt the timing mechanism was intuitive (for me) but even if it's harder to understand timing, the game is forgiving if you save often. And who wouldn't save often, when to do so you must pet a cat (which heals you entirely)?!? Even if grinding out battles doesn't help you with the timing, and you hate the battles, you can just turn on "auto victory" and tap out when the going gets tough. Another reason to promote is for the puzzles. Golden Sun is one of my all-time favorite games and I have been searching for a long time for a game that emulates those out-of-battle puzzle mechanics; Ikenfell comes close, with the hidden rooms/pathways and logic puzzles (though sadly not as focused on interacting with the environment as G.S.). Lastly, if you are an LGBTQIA+ person (or ally) I would highly recommend supporting this game: the characters are well-written, spanning the spectrum, and the banter is charming. We need more games like this!

representative_reviews.title: Ikenfell
representative_reviews.text: This game is extremely cute! All the characters are lovely and their queerness is apparent without overshadowing the rest of their personalities. The story is very interesting and has strong emotional beats, though the plotting is occasionally a little messy. The high points more than balance out the low ones though and the game's conclusion and character arcs were very satisfying. I enjoyed the battle system, which was a mix of grid-based tactical RPG party combat and Paper Mario-style action commands. Each party member has their own move set with unique timings, range, and area of effect. Figuring out who to bring and how to use them effectively in each fight is very satisfying. The game has a bit of a steep difficulty curve as enemies (especially bosses) ramp up their damage very fast if you can't do blocks with good timing, but healing is plentiful and the ability to restart a fight immediately after losing helps to make re-doing tough fights less frustrating. Since enemies can be encountered (or avoided) in the overworld to start battles, I was hoping to have some sort of first-strike system to get an edge going into a fight, but that didn't seem to be available. Overall, I had a great time with this game, both in the main story and in the handful of secret side trips lurking around. Highly recommend to anyone who is a fan of action-command RPGs and queer witches.

representative_reviews.title: ELDEN RING
representative_reviews.text: [h1]Probably the biggest letdown of a game.[/h1] I have to preface this and say that this is my first soulslike experience. Elden ring videos and players promise hard gameplay, great story, and cinematic experience. In reality? It's [b]unmeasurable disappointment[/b] on several fronts. My first issue is that this game was supposed to be made for controllers. You'd think with controllers your movement would be optimized with omnidirectional movement, variable speed, etc. No. No it is not. Too simple of concepts for these simple devs. In order to sprint in this game you have to hold the same button you dodge with (B as I'm on Xbox controller). So if you were to do something as simple as dodge while running, you have to hold the direction and quickly release and tap your dodge button again. This is already awkard of a movement and you'd think it'd be fixed in early builds of the game. Nada. On top of this awkward movement, your dodge actually only starts once the dodge button is released. This wonderfully stupid idea of a mechanic makes reactive playstyles (what'd you'd expect to play as a game centered around boss fights) useless. The amount of time it takes for you to actually do what you inputed is elongated by dumb design. This leads to another problem later on. [i]I'm just gonna forego the horrible auto-lock and let other players tell you about that dumpster fire.[/i] My second issue is FPS being locked. 60hz is stone age. People have to spend $60 to get this game (crazy ik). When you can get a 60+fps monitor for $80. Let's think here, are your customers going to say "God I hope this cinematic game is locked at 60fps". Seriously unless you're a foot in the grave you can see the slop that is 60 fps. Did you buy a actual monitor? Something beyond 60fps? Yikes you're going to see some stuttering if your hz isn't divisible by 60 f*cking fps or has freesync. Now in the defense of this game, I understand that the game is based around the 60fps for engine reasons and for console players. Yet, WHY is it 60 fps when ported to PC. I'm writing this review 4 years later and there is still no support for higher framerates. Dollar per frame game. My third issue, difficulty. This game isn't "hard", it's tedious. I started playing this game in hopes of dodging bosses last second, paying attention to a flurry of attacks as they came out, and getting bested because I lacked the mechanical skill to beat a boss. Reality? This game has THE MOST BORING BOSS FIGHTS. Let me explain. Every boss has movepools. Which when learned make the boss easier, but Elden Ring makes it BORING. However, the fun should lie in going against new bosses right? Maybe getting lucky and beating them first try? Well unless it's one of the billion copy print dungeons with bosses that might as well be 2D for the lack of depth to them, you're going to die (probably in those dungeons too). You'll be hit with a move you can't properly dodge because well you've never seen it before.Or even worse, you have yet the timing is slightly different, with extensions of range or attack(s). Some people may not have a problem with this whole "see a new move, die and come back pattern". And to those people I say, "Keep flipping those burgers." The allure in bossfighting games is making yourself a betterplayer. One able to become better in any situation as you progress. Not dying 2-3, 4 times before you get the boss to a next phase where you'll have to repeat the same steps. This loop? It's not skillful dodges, parrying, or anything cool like that. It's just dying, learning, and coming back. That is profoundly boring. If all your bosses can just simply be put into a youtube video devolving strategies to counter every situation, you didn't make a skillfull game, you made a knowledge gap. [u]Seriously the bosses might as well be a quizlet looking at each boss's attacks like flashcards and memorizing.[/u] And you'd know I'd take it all back if the story was redeeming. Stories can carry bad gameplay after all. But truth be told you won't really even learn the story in this game. You have to go OUT of your way to find what this game is about. Other RPGs I've played such as Fallout 4, Cyberpunk 2077, Pokémon, all find ways to sprinkle in story if you just go a little bit off the game's main course. This game? You pretty much need a guide to get a inkling of it at all. You will have many questions when the game starts and as it progresses, you'll just have more and more. It's hard to find motivation to do quests with characters you know nothing about. This game doesn't motivate you to do anything, you pop in the world, you look around a bit, and you're confused. I understand that it is a game for adults, so make the story a bit complex. However at the start of the game, you as a protagonist get the sole goal of becoming the Elden Lord from a good cutscene. Now it may just be me, but [u]why does it sound like we're setting up a tv show?[/u] Could it be that it just said a bunch of characters nobody knows, gave the tiniest amount of backstory that you don't really understand, and had a vague direction? Maybe...maybe. But surely this is a good story. It will tell you a bit more as you start the game... Yeah no, this game has bad storytelling. Not necessarily a bad story I hear if you have thousands of hours to waste reading every item, replaying for minute things you missed because the game [b] Doesn't Have Story Direction [/b]. My advice F-Soft, narrow the guage just a little bit more so people can know why they should give a crap. Then the whole discover the lore thing works. But hey, if all that sounds appealing to you, go ahead and pay your $60 for 60fps. Have fun wasting your time memorizing an interactive textbook everyone else has already read, memorized, condensed, and posted the results of online. Edit 1: I've since beat Elden Ring and it was unfulfilling. I have yet to play the DLC (got a gamekey bundle for cheap). At this point in time everything still stands. Play modded if you can. But unless you're an achievement hunter like me, better steer clear, there's some enjoyable moments in this game, but the bad camera control, crappy controls, and 60fps still make this game hard to enjoy. It's sad that unpaid modders make the fixes that paid devs couldn't. That said, if you have a fit girl you know, go there. Don't buy.

representative_reviews.title: ELDEN RING
representative_reviews.text: so at 3/4 of 1k hrs into this game i feel i have the ability to leave a actual worth while review for it. To start this off, i will say this is the easiest Soulslike to get into and i adore how it lets you either do everything or do minimal, not only because some of us just arent completionists but also because it helps if you Elden ring RP like i do in my own little head canon at times. The only two main negatives i can say anything about are the two that make my eyes rollll playthrough after playthrough. horse combat Boss variety. representative_reviews.title: Meg's Monster
representative_reviews.text: A heartfelt story that visually might be very reminiscent of another game that features monster and human tensions, but it stands out with a nice focus on a set main cast that I couldn't help but just adore. Pretty good Pixel art, nice colour palettes that set the mood. With a mix of overworld sprites and more detailed combat sprites, the latter while not being the most animated compared to the former, I welcomed them to break the story from time to time. Combat. Every fight being unique, going the route of every fight is a boss rather than a random enemy. Most if not all of the fights have a unique THING going on to try and not be a repetitive turn based game, this is more expanded on in later fights Beautiful soundtrack, hitting the right notes in the correct places, though I felt it's a little limited and not too memorable, but that's purely personal. The combat feels a little tagged on, while there is variety in the enemies you typically only fight once, game overs tend to fall down to extremely bad luck since you are on a linear path with no real options besides your established mechanics. How the player avoids a game over, I'd say it's at least unique, so a bonus for that. Despite having a world map, the game is purely linear (you are pretty much locked into your linear route too) With no real reason to explore any place further outside of areas being no more than 2-3 rooms large at most points. Side quests don't really add much bulk to the game play or plot, with one side quest being awkwardly placed tone wise and the other being multiple side quests that seem almost shoe-horned in to bulk up the plot and twist (or someone just REALLY liked a certain character idk lol) While I think the ending is certainly a nice one, some elements of the plot and characters could've been explored more, the setting of the world REALLY should've been explored more, certain plot points I have either missed or the game didn't bother to tell me. (If it's left up to interpretation then that's totally fine) I feel the game could've just been MORE that what it already is if it was given more time to work on rather than a nice little shortened story to get done in a few hours. Despite what I feel, I do think it was a cute little game, However I would REALLY recommend one buys it SUPER discounted or just watch someone else play it, you will both share the same experience. I just don't think the price is worth a 5-7 hour experience. I'd like to recommend it but it's just lacking in content and replayability.

representative_reviews.title: Ikenfell
representative_reviews.text: A monotonously unimaginative narrative, strung along by an upsettingly tedious and shallow combat system. The novelty of the colourful pixel world and tile-based combat system are fine at first, but only get worse as the game rolls out more content to reveal there's no more depth to the experience than that. The combat system is not very tactical at all. Every single combat encounter the map is the exact same three by twelve grid with no obstacles or hazards or anything. Every single map is just that. All the player does is move the characters in range of the enemies on this confined, barren grid and then chunk out the same damage skills over and over again. To artificially make the experience more engaging players need to perform a quick time event every single time they use an ability or are attacked. These quick time events drastically impact the outcome of each turn and encounter as a whole. Missing the quick time will generally result in an enemy attack dealing triple damage compared to pressing at the very last moment for the most reduction. Same goes for when the player controlled characters attack, it will be anything from a fraction to full damage based on the quick time event. Players have to do this quick time event for every single action in every single combat encounter throughout what is probably a fifteen or more hour campaign. And every single new enemy attack and new character ability has a completely different timing, sometimes it's about when the hit lands other times it's a fraction of a second after the hit lands other times it's not the hit at all it's based on some random other part of the animation. At first it's not so bad but after over ten hours of combat which is only engaging because quick time events force the player to pay attention, it's exhausting and unfun. The map layout is the same every fight, there's barely even any room to move around in, there's no dynamic strategies or synergies between items and abilities, players have minimal access to buffs or control affects that allow for actually strategy, there's little players can do to tactically respond or counter or account for enemy actions at all in any way, and players have to take up a whole turn if they want to use an item so items are a waste of time outside of higher difficulty fights. If players don't waste time fighting against anything other than the boss, then players end up being underpowered for the boss fight and have to waste ridiculous amounts of time chipping the boss down; which negates all the time the player saved from skipping the previous fights. There doesn't seem to be much variety in gearing for statistics either since players can't really focus anything enough to make a huge difference, although without speed enemies will start taking multiple turns before the player gets to. Admittedly the game does actually give players a toggle in the settings menu to allow for instantly winning combat and, I think, bypassing the quick time events as well. But if entire core mechanics of the game need to be removed just to make it less unfun then that's a problem. Similarly to the combat, at first the story is also decent if not especially exciting. But it doesn't get anymore exciting as it advances. The world is just a bunch of bland, unimaginative copy paste magic whatever. Nothing special, nothing unique or creative about any of it. The lore of how the world was created gets even worse. Arbitrarily large whale, mammoths and a raven who for some reason have the ability and desire to create things; created things. That's it that's the universe lore. Same with the plot, it does try to at least do something different yet it's still just a vague asinine problem that has a vague asinine solution and overtime it just becomes less vague. None of the twists the plot provides in twelve hours are actually exciting, especially because most of the specific details that the plot revolves around are arbitrarily thrown at the player out of nowhere; and the player just has to nod along. The characters are about the same. Not awful, but not unique or interesting either. Very copy paste predictable personality categories without much depth beyond that initial category. Half of the characters either don't have any major drama problems but also supply absolutely no reason for the player to be interested or intrigued by their existence at all; while the other characters do have drama problems but it's all petty obnoxious issues that make zero sense to be showing up in the middle of such a drastic world saving whatever plot. The most consistently fresh aspect of the game is simply just running around the world collecting items and advancing from room to room while solving mild puzzles. The game has decent pixel graphics and fairly diverse, if not still uninspired, environments along with a solid amount of nice music. The select few songs that actually have sung lyrics tend to be shallowly written and extremely out of place though. Ironically the least music variety appears to be in combat. Players get to listen to the same song for the fiftieth time while performing the same quick time event for the two hundredth time. As referenced I was genuinely fine with the game at first. But after twelve hours of the same quick time events, the same empty maps; the only reason combat even started becoming especially difficult was because the characters had become underpowered due to me desperately avoiding enemy encounters to save time, and I actually started missing quick time events more often because of how tired I got of doing them. Meanwhile the story just keeps going on with the same inane fantasy save the world discover the boring details of the predictable secrets and now one of the characters is having a tantrum again so time to stop everything for them before immediately resuming once the petty social crisis is over. There's just nothing new about this in terms of gameplay or story. Yet it's over twelve hours long and demands constant attention from the player the whole way despite not providing anything of genuine intrigue. This game actually would of benefited from being much, much shorter. If you're interested in finding some games that I do positively recommend they can be found on my curator page [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/38950844-Anoemalous/] here [/url].

representative_reviews.text: Final Update : Worse then I could have imagined. No pay off for the end. Final boss is a "out of no where" but also not really and it's a big let down. They gloss over any actual impact the end could have had for a non-offensive ending. If everyone in this world is gay, how do they keep the population? Come on guys, you want inclusion but you didn't actually have inclusion. That aside, the game-play is good and the only thing that carries the game. Seeing Ze and Zir is just so out of place. My theory was not correct but would have been a much better and dramatic ending, you know actual writing! Why is the last boss easier then the 2nd to last boss? The "lost sister" has no pay off and she doesn't deserve the happy ending she got because there was only a few scenes showing her that were there to make you think something else. I did call/predict the one twist that came true at the very very end after the credits. (Like I said predictable but also not predictable but in a very bad way) Oh and the end credits song... wow what a pile of ♥♥♥♥♥. Why did only a few of the characters get lyrics in their "theme song"... I could go on for paragraphs but I'll stop, it's not worth my time. I never give scores but for this I have to. Story 1/10 Game-play 9/10. Update 2 : Yet it still manages to be worse. I thought it was very predictable before and it just keeps NOT surprising me because I can tell what's going to happen. Also just about every other character is just so badly written and cookie cutter forced to be "non-conforming" it's laughable. I mean if you want to do inclusion at least TRY and be good about it. The game-play is the ONLY reason I'm still playing. Update : Oh god the writing got worse! At least the combat is fun. Mixed so far. Most of the characters are annoying and VERY cookie cutter stereotypes. Also why is it that everyone in the game has to be LGBT? Look, I'm an ally and all but come on, not everyone is "gender fluid". You want inclusion, I get that, that's great. However that also means you need some other types in there too. You go all in like that and it just feels forced. Also why are kids/very young teens constantly saying someone else is cute or hot? Needless to say the writing is pretty rough. Gameplay is ok so far. Some annoying enemies.

representative_reviews.text: Amazing. It's such an incredibly well made experience - because it's so tight and focused, as it's promising. There's no artificial game stretching, no grinding. It's a pretty focused game - but because of that controlled nature, it shines. The writing is great, story events are flowing, rewards and progression are tied to the story (and not random grind). There is place for things going non-linear, with a little bit of tasks and side quests, but it's all nicely tied together. The world is just well designed, fantasy adjusted to reality of rodents - giving the same vibe as Kingdoms of The Dump, playing with a different perspective on the world and doing it in many creative ways. It's a joy to play, even if this is not a very challenging experience difficulty wise - but it's just your own fable story that you can't put down.

representative_reviews.title: In Stars And Time
representative_reviews.text: I really wanted to like this one but found the writing overly self-conscious, and the gameplay eventually started to drag near the end. If one or the other was more compelling, I would have enjoyed it. It's very polished and there are a lot of neat ideas!! And I can imagine younger folks finding more in the character dynamics. But just not for me at this point in my life.

representative_reviews.title: To the Moon
representative_reviews.text: It's not worth the hype. I have played 45 minutes so far in one sitting and there isn't really anything making me want to continue, gameplay or story-wise. The dialogues in this game physically hurt me.. and I played throughout the whole House in Fata Morgana and loved it so that's saying something. I get from where the positive reviews are coming from (and there is likely more to this game that I haven't discovered yet), but I just did not enjoy the experience. The overly in-your-face simplicity and storytelling just don't make for an enjoyable experience, along with a linear design that tries hard to feel like exploration but in the end leaves you feeling trapped gameplay wise in a non-engaging loop. With all that, I am glad that so many people found it beautiful and it brought wamth to them. And glad that I tried it to see for myself.
